questions.question: Propositional logic is the simplest form of logic in which all statements are represented as:
questions.explanation: In propositional logic every statement is represented as a proposition.

questions.question: A proposition is a declarative statement that is:
questions.explanation: A proposition is a declarative statement that is either True or False.

questions.question: Propositional logic is also called:
questions.explanation: PL is called Boolean logic because it works with 0 (False) and 1 (True).

questions.question: Which of the following is a proposition?
questions.explanation: Only a declarative statement with a truth value is a proposition, and "5 is a prime number" is True.

questions.question: The truth value of "The Sun rises from the West" is:
questions.explanation: The statement is a proposition and its truth value is False.

questions.question: Which symbol represents negation (NOT)?
questions.explanation: Negation is written ¬ (or ~).

questions.question: The symbol ∧ represents:
questions.explanation: ∧ stands for conjunction, which means AND.

questions.question: The symbol ∨ represents:
questions.explanation: ∨ stands for disjunction, which means OR.

questions.question: The symbol → represents:
questions.explanation: → stands for implication, read "if P, then Q".

questions.question: The symbol ⇔ (or ↔) represents:
questions.explanation: ⇔ stands for the biconditional, read "if and only if".

questions.question: Logical connectives are also called:
questions.explanation: The notes say logical connectives are also called logical operators.

questions.question: How many main logical connectives are described in the notes?
questions.explanation: The five connectives are negation, conjunction, disjunction, implication and biconditional.

questions.question: An atomic proposition is:

options.B: A simple proposition made of a single proposition symbol

questions.explanation: An atomic proposition is a single symbol such as P, Q or R.

questions.question: A compound proposition is formed by:

options.A: Combining two or more atomic propositions using logical connectives

questions.explanation: Compound propositions join atomic propositions with connectives.

questions.question: If P = "It is raining", then ¬P is:
questions.explanation: ¬P is the negation of P, so it states the opposite.

questions.question: A literal is:

options.D: Either a positive literal P or a negative literal ¬P

questions.explanation: A literal is a positive literal (P) or a negative literal (¬P).

questions.question: Two propositions are logically equivalent when:

options.B: Their truth-table columns are identical for all possible values
options.C: They have the same number of connectives

questions.explanation: Logical equivalence means identical truth-table columns.

questions.question: Which symbol is used to write logical equivalence?
questions.explanation: Logical equivalence is written P ≡ Q.

questions.question: In AI, inference is the process of:

options.D: Generating new conclusions from existing facts or evidence

questions.explanation: Inference derives conclusions from facts or evidence.

questions.question: Inference rules are:

options.C: Templates used to generate valid arguments

questions.explanation: Inference rules are templates for producing valid arguments and proofs.

questions.question: Which rule says: from P → Q and P, conclude Q?
questions.explanation: This is Modus Ponens.

questions.question: Which rule says: from P → Q and ¬Q, conclude ¬P?
questions.explanation: This is Modus Tollens.

questions.question: Which rule says: from P → Q and Q → R, conclude P → R?
questions.explanation: This is Hypothetical Syllogism.

questions.question: Which rule says: from P ∨ Q and ¬P, conclude Q?
questions.explanation: This is Disjunctive Syllogism.

questions.question: Which rule says: from P, conclude P ∨ Q?
questions.explanation: This is the Addition rule.

questions.question: Which rule says: from P ∧ Q, conclude P?
questions.explanation: This is the Simplification rule.

questions.question: How many inference rules of propositional logic are listed in the notes?
questions.explanation: The notes list seven rules from Modus Ponens to Resolution.

questions.question: The converse of P → Q is:
questions.explanation: The converse swaps the two sides: Q → P.

questions.question: The contrapositive of P → Q is:
questions.explanation: The contrapositive swaps and negates both parts: ¬Q → ¬P.

questions.question: The inverse of P → Q is:
questions.explanation: The inverse negates both parts: ¬P → ¬Q.

questions.question: A fallacy is:

options.C: An error in reasoning that makes an argument invalid or unreliable

questions.explanation: A fallacy is an error in reasoning, even if the argument looks convincing.

questions.question: First-Order Logic is also called:
questions.explanation: FOL is also called predicate logic or First-Order Predicate Logic (FOPL).

questions.question: First-Order Logic is an extension of:
questions.explanation: FOL extends propositional logic.

questions.question: A semantic network is a graph in which:

options.A: Nodes stand for objects or concepts and arcs stand for relations

questions.explanation: A semantic network represents objects or concepts as nodes and relations as labelled arcs.

questions.question: Which is an example of a unary relation in FOL?
questions.explanation: A unary relation involves one object, such as red or round.

questions.question: Which of the following is a function symbol in the FOL syntax table of the notes?
questions.explanation: sqrt and LeftLegOf are the function examples, while Brother and > are predicates.

questions.question: The goal of the Water Jug problem in the notes is to get exactly:
questions.explanation: The notes use a 4 L and a 3 L jug with the goal of 2 litres in the 4 L jug.

questions.question: A frame stores knowledge about an object or situation as a set of:
questions.explanation: A frame consists of slots (attributes) and fillers (values).

questions.question: Variables in FOL represent:
questions.explanation: Variables such as x, y, z represent unknown or general objects.

questions.question: Predicates in FOL represent:
questions.explanation: Predicates represent properties or relationships, such as Brother or Father.

questions.question: The quantifier ∀ means:
questions.explanation: ∀ is the universal quantifier, "for all".

questions.question: The quantifier ∃ means:
questions.explanation: ∃ is the existential quantifier, "there exists".

questions.question: The general form of an atomic sentence in FOL is:
questions.explanation: An atomic sentence is a predicate applied to one or more terms.

questions.question: Cat(Chinky) is an example of:
questions.explanation: It is a predicate with one term, so it is an atomic sentence.

questions.question: Complex sentences in FOL are formed by:

options.B: Combining atomic sentences with logical connectives

questions.explanation: Complex sentences combine two or more atomic sentences with connectives.

questions.question: Prolog stands for:
questions.explanation: Prolog is short for PROgramming in LOGic.

questions.question: Prolog is a:
questions.explanation: Prolog is a declarative language based on a subset of first-order logic.

questions.question: A thematic role frame represents the meaning of a sentence as:

options.C: An event with roles played by participants

questions.explanation: A thematic role frame stores an event and the roles of its participants.

questions.question: A production rule has the form:
questions.explanation: A production rule is an IF-THEN rule.

questions.question: Logic is best described as:
questions.explanation: The notes define logic as the science of correct reasoning.

questions.question: According to the notes, the basic elements of propositional logic are:
questions.explanation: The notes correct slide 19: propositions and connectives are the basic elements of PL.

questions.question: "It is raining today and the street is wet" with P = raining and Q = street wet is written:
questions.explanation: "And" is conjunction, so the statement is P ∧ Q.

questions.question: "Ritika is a doctor or engineer" is an example of:
questions.explanation: The word "or" shows disjunction (∨).

questions.question: "I am breathing if and only if I am alive" is an example of:
questions.explanation: "If and only if" is the biconditional ⇔.

questions.question: Negation may also be written with which symbol?
questions.explanation: The notes say negation may be written as ~ (slide 30).

questions.question: The implication P → Q is False only when:

options.A: P is True and Q is False
options.B: P is False and Q is True
options.C: Both P and Q are False
options.D: Both P and Q are True

questions.explanation: From the truth table, P → Q is False only in the row T, F.

questions.question: The disjunction P ∨ Q is False only when:

options.A: Both P and Q are False
options.D: Exactly one of them is True

questions.explanation: An OR is false only when both parts are false.

questions.question: The conjunction P ∧ Q is True only when:

options.A: At least one of them is True
options.C: P is False and Q is True
options.D: Both P and Q are True

questions.explanation: An AND is true only when both parts are true.

questions.question: ¬A ∨ B is logically equivalent to:
questions.explanation: The truth table shows ¬A ∨ B and A → B have identical columns.

questions.question: Which statement shows commutativity?
questions.explanation: Commutativity means the order of operands does not matter.

questions.question: De Morgan's law for ¬(P ∧ Q) gives:
De Morgan's law for ¬(P ∨ Q) gives:
Double-negation elimination states that:
questions.explanation: Negating twice returns the original proposition.

questions.question: Which is the distributive law?
questions.explanation: The distributive law spreads ∧ over ∨, and ∨ over ∧.

questions.question: The equation P ∨ True = True is usually called the:
questions.explanation: The notes point out that slide 32 calls it the identity element, but it is usually the domination law.

questions.question: The identity law for OR is:
questions.explanation: The identity law for OR is P ∨ False = P.

questions.question: Which of these can propositional logic NOT represent properly?
questions.explanation: PL cannot represent ALL, some or none statements.

questions.question: Why is First-Order Logic needed?

options.B: PL has limited expressive power and cannot represent complex statements or detailed relationships
options.C: PL cannot be True or False

questions.explanation: PL limits make a more powerful logic necessary.

questions.question: "Some apples are sweet" cannot be written properly in PL because PL:
questions.explanation: PL has no way to express quantities like all, some or none.

questions.question: The components of a production system are:

options.D: Production rules, working memory and control strategy

questions.explanation: A production system has a rule set, a working memory (global database) and a control strategy.

questions.question: Which pair of forms is logically equivalent?
questions.explanation: The implication is equivalent to its contrapositive.

questions.question: The converse Q → P is logically equivalent to:
questions.explanation: From the truth table, the converse and inverse have identical columns.

questions.question: An implication P → Q is NOT equivalent to:
questions.explanation: The implication is not equivalent to its converse or inverse.

questions.question: Which memory trick describes the contrapositive?

options.C: Swap the sides AND negate both

questions.explanation: Contrapositive = swap and negate both, so it is always equivalent to the original.

questions.question: "If I am sleepy then I go to bed. I am sleepy." The conclusion by Modus Ponens is:

options.C: I do not go to bed

questions.explanation: Modus Ponens gives Q, so "I go to bed".

questions.question: "If I am sleepy then I go to bed. I do not go to bed." The conclusion by Modus Tollens is:
questions.explanation: Modus Tollens gives ¬P, so "I am not sleepy".

questions.question: "If you have my home key you can unlock my home. If you can unlock my home you can take my money." Hypothetical Syllogism concludes:

options.C: If you have my home key then you can take my money

questions.explanation: Hypothetical Syllogism gives P → R.

questions.question: "Today is Sunday or Monday. Today is not Sunday." Disjunctive Syllogism concludes:
questions.explanation: From P ∨ Q and ¬P, we get Q.

questions.question: The correct resolution rule is:

options.D: P → Q, Q → R ∴ P → R

questions.explanation: Resolution resolves complementary literals P and ¬P from two clauses.

questions.question: What correction do the notes make to slide 44 on Resolution?

options.A: The conclusion should be Q ∧ R
options.B: The first premise should be P ∧ Q
options.D: The second premise should be ¬P ∨ R, not ¬P ∧ R

questions.explanation: The standard rule uses OR in both premises.

questions.question: Common sense reasoning is difficult for AI because:

options.D: Everyday knowledge is huge, rarely written down and has exceptions

questions.explanation: The notes list large volume, exceptions (like penguins) and reasoning about time, space and cause.

questions.question: The fallacy "P → Q, Q therefore P" is called:
questions.explanation: Concluding P from Q in P → Q is affirming the consequent, which is invalid.

questions.question: The fallacy "P → Q, ¬P therefore ¬Q" is called:
questions.explanation: Concluding ¬Q from ¬P is denying the antecedent, which is invalid.

questions.question: An ad hominem fallacy:

options.A: Draws a conclusion from too few cases
options.B: Attacks the person, not the argument
options.C: Assumes the conclusion in a premise

questions.explanation: Ad hominem attacks the person instead of the argument.

questions.question: A hasty generalisation is a conclusion drawn from:
questions.explanation: It generalises from too few examples.

questions.question: Circular reasoning is when:

options.C: The conclusion is already assumed in a premise

questions.explanation: Circular reasoning assumes what it tries to prove.

questions.question: A false dilemma is when:

options.A: Only two choices are shown although more exist
options.B: A conclusion is based on too few cases

questions.explanation: The false dilemma presents only two options.

questions.question: Which list gives the ways of knowledge representation in the notes?

options.A: Truth table, clause, literal and tableau
options.D: Logical representation, semantic network, frames and production rules

questions.explanation: The four ways are logical representation, semantic networks, frames and production rules.

questions.question: Who proposed frames, according to the notes?
questions.explanation: The notes credit frames to Marvin Minsky.

questions.question: The knowledge engineering process described in the notes has how many stages?
questions.explanation: Knowledge engineering has seven stages (Russell and Norvig).

questions.question: The first stage of knowledge engineering is:
questions.explanation: The process begins by identifying the task.

questions.question: The last stage of knowledge engineering is:
questions.explanation: The seventh stage is debugging the knowledge base.

questions.question: Unlike PL, FOL assumes the world contains:

options.B: Facts, objects, properties and relationships between objects

questions.explanation: FOL assumes objects, properties and relationships in addition to facts.

questions.question: Partitioned semantic nets are used mainly to represent:
questions.explanation: Spaces let partitioned nets show ∀, ∃, negation and beliefs.

questions.question: Which FOL element shows that two values or objects are equal?
questions.explanation: Equality is the element written with =.

questions.question: In the semantic net example, to find out whether Tom has fur you follow:

options.C: Tom → Cat → Mammal and read "has Fur"

questions.explanation: Inheritance lets Tom take the properties of Cat, Mammal and Animal.

questions.question: The parallel implementation of semantic nets works by:

options.C: Marker passing or spreading activation along links in parallel

questions.explanation: Markers travel along is-a links in parallel, and the answer is yes if they meet.

questions.question: In a thematic role frame, the Agent is:
questions.explanation: The agent is the doer of the action.

questions.question: The usual pattern for the universal quantifier is:
questions.explanation: The notes give ∀x (P(x) ⇒ Q(x)) as the usual pattern.

questions.question: The usual pattern for the existential quantifier is:
questions.explanation: The notes give ∃x (P(x) ∧ Q(x)) as the usual pattern.

questions.question: When P is False and Q is True, the value of P → Q is:
questions.explanation: An implication is False only when P is True and Q is False, so here it is True.

questions.question: When P is True and Q is False, the value of P ⇔ Q is:
questions.explanation: A biconditional is True only when P and Q have the same value.

questions.question: When both P and Q are False, the value of P ⇔ Q is:
questions.explanation: Both values are the same, so the biconditional is True.

questions.question: When P is False and Q is True, the converse Q → P has the value:
questions.explanation: Q is True and P is False, so Q → P is False.

questions.question: When P is True and Q is False, the contrapositive ¬Q → ¬P has the value:
questions.explanation: ¬Q is True and ¬P is False, so the contrapositive is False, matching P → Q.

questions.question: When P is False and Q is True, the inverse ¬P → ¬Q has the value:
questions.explanation: ¬P is True and ¬Q is False, so the inverse is False.

questions.question: In the sentence "Sita gave a book to Amit in the library", the Recipient is:
questions.explanation: Amit receives the book, so he is the Recipient.

questions.question: The true negation of P → Q is:
questions.explanation: The notes say the true negation of P → Q is P ∧ ¬Q.

questions.question: What does the notes' remark on slide 36 say about the contrapositive?

options.A: It is the negation of P → Q
options.C: It is the converse with both parts negated
options.D: It is not equivalent to P → Q

questions.explanation: The notes explain that the contrapositive is strictly the converse with both parts negated.

questions.question: "If it rains, the street is wet. The street is not wet." The valid conclusion is:
questions.explanation: Modus Tollens gives ¬P: it did not rain.

questions.question: "If it rains, the street is wet. The street is wet. So it rained." This reasoning is:

options.B: The fallacy of affirming the consequent

questions.explanation: The street may be wet for another reason, so this is affirming the consequent.

questions.question: "If it rains, the street is wet. It is not raining. So the street is not wet." This reasoning is:

options.A: The fallacy of denying the antecedent

questions.explanation: It treats the inverse as if it were the implication, so it is invalid.

questions.question: "I have a vanilla ice-cream. So I have vanilla or chocolate ice-cream." Which rule is used?
questions.explanation: From P we get P ∨ Q, which is the Addition rule.

questions.question: "Rohan is intelligent and hardworking. So Rohan is intelligent." Which rule is used?
questions.explanation: From P ∧ Q we get P, which is Simplification.

questions.question: "It is Sunday or a holiday. It is not Sunday or I am free. So it is a holiday or I am free." Which rule is used?
questions.explanation: P ∨ Q and ¬P ∨ R give Q ∨ R, which is Resolution.

questions.question: Why is affirming the consequent invalid?

options.B: It treats the converse Q → P as if it were the implication P → Q

questions.explanation: The notes explain it confuses the converse with the implication.

questions.question: The contrapositive of "If it is raining, then the street is wet" is:

options.A: If the street is wet, then it is raining
options.B: If it is not raining, then the street is not wet
options.C: If it is raining, then the street is not wet
options.D: If the street is not wet, then it is not raining

questions.explanation: The contrapositive is ¬Q → ¬P.

questions.question: The inverse of "If it is raining, then the street is wet" is:

options.A: If the street is not wet, then it is not raining
options.B: If the street is wet, then it is raining
options.C: If it is not raining, then the street is not wet
options.D: If it is raining, then the street is dry

questions.explanation: The inverse is ¬P → ¬Q.

questions.question: The converse of "If it is raining, then the street is wet" is:

options.A: If the street is not wet, then it is not raining
options.B: If the street is wet, then it is raining
options.C: If it is not raining, then the street is not wet
options.D: If it is raining, then the street is wet

questions.explanation: The converse is Q → P.

questions.question: "All the girls are intelligent" is written in FOL as:
questions.explanation: The universal quantifier is used with implication.

questions.question: "Some apples are sweet" is written in FOL as:
questions.explanation: The existential quantifier is used with conjunction.

questions.question: "No apple is sweet" is written in FOL as:
questions.explanation: The notes write it as ∀x (Apple(x) ⇒ ¬Sweet(x)).

questions.question: In the semantic net example, which link joins Tom to Cat?
questions.explanation: Tom is an individual, so he is linked to his class by instance-of, while Cat is linked to Mammal by is-a.

questions.question: ¬∀x P(x) is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: Not all objects satisfy P means some object does not satisfy P.

questions.question: ¬∃x P(x) is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: If no object satisfies P, then every object fails P.

questions.question: To prove an argument valid with a semantic tableau, we assume that:

options.A: The premises are false and the conclusion is true
options.B: The premises are true and the conclusion is false
options.C: Both premises and conclusion are false

questions.explanation: A tableau is a refutation method, starting from true premises and a false conclusion.

questions.question: In a semantic tableau, the argument is valid when:

options.A: At least one branch stays open
options.B: The tree has only one branch
options.D: Every branch closes with a contradiction

questions.explanation: If every branch contains P and ¬P, the assumption is impossible and the argument is valid.

questions.question: The tableau rule for P ∨ Q is to:

options.A: Add P and Q on the same branch
options.C: Split into two branches, one with P and one with Q

questions.explanation: A disjunction splits the tableau into two branches.

questions.question: The tableau rule for P → Q is to:

options.A: Add P and Q on the same branch
options.D: Split into two branches, one with ¬P and one with Q

questions.explanation: An implication is treated as ¬P ∨ Q, so it splits into ¬P and Q.

questions.question: The tableau rule for ¬(P ∨ Q) is to:

options.B: Add ¬P and ¬Q on the same branch

questions.explanation: By De Morgan, ¬(P ∨ Q) = ¬P ∧ ¬Q, so both are added on the same branch.

questions.question: The first step of resolution in propositional logic is to:
questions.explanation: The first step converts all statements into clauses.

questions.question: In resolution, the goal is proved when:
questions.explanation: Deriving the empty clause shows a contradiction, so the goal is proved.

questions.question: Resolving the clauses (¬P ∨ Q) and P gives:
questions.explanation: P and ¬P cancel, leaving Q.

questions.question: In FOPL resolution, unification means:

options.A: Finding a substitution that makes two literals identical

questions.explanation: Unification matches variables so that literals can be resolved.

questions.question: Skolemisation replaces:

options.B: Each ∃ variable by a new constant (or a function of the ∀ variables)

questions.explanation: Skolemisation removes existential quantifiers.

questions.question: A FOL tableau may not terminate because:

options.C: FOL is the same as PL

questions.explanation: A proof is found if the statement is valid, but the search may run forever if it is not.

questions.question: The rule Grandparent(x, z) ⇔ ∃y (Parent(x, y) ∧ Parent(y, z)) means:

options.A: x is a grandparent of z if x is a parent of someone who is a parent of z
options.B: x is a parent of z
options.C: z is a parent of x

questions.explanation: The rule says a grandparent is a parent of a parent.

questions.question: In Prolog, the symbol :- means:
questions.explanation: :- means "if", a comma means AND and a semicolon means OR.

questions.question: In the Student frame example, Ravi gets Course = BCA because:

options.B: An instance inherits default slot values from its frame

questions.explanation: Instances inherit defaults from the frame.

questions.question: In the Water Jug solution, the first step from (0, 0) using R2 gives:
questions.explanation: R2 fills the 3 L jug, so (0, 0) becomes (0, 3).

questions.question: In the Water Jug solution, from (3, 3) pouring into the 4 L jug until it is full gives:
questions.explanation: The 4 L jug needs 1 more litre, so 1 L moves and 2 L remains in the 3 L jug.

questions.question: In the Water Jug solution of the notes, how many moves reach the goal (2, 0)?
questions.explanation: The solution goes through six moves ending at (2, 0).

questions.question: The shortest solution of the Missionaries and Cannibals problem in the notes has how many crossings?
questions.explanation: The notes give a solution of 11 crossings.

questions.question: In the Missionaries and Cannibals problem, the safety constraint is that:

options.A: On a bank that has missionaries, the cannibals must not outnumber them
options.B: The boat must carry exactly three people
options.C: Missionaries must always outnumber cannibals on both banks, even empty ones

questions.explanation: The cannibals must not outnumber missionaries on any bank where missionaries are present.

questions.question: Which placement is a valid solution of the 4-Queen problem (row, column)?
questions.explanation: Only the first placement has no two queens in the same column or diagonal.

questions.question: For which values of n does the n-Queen problem have no solution, according to the notes?
questions.explanation: The notes say n = 2 and n = 3 have no solution.

questions.question: What is the correct order of actions in the Monkey and Banana solution?

options.A: Climb on the box, walk, push, grasp
options.C: Push the box, walk, grasp, climb
options.D: Walk to the box, push it under the banana, climb on it, grasp the banana

questions.explanation: The monkey walks A to B, pushes the box to C, climbs and then grasps.

questions.question: In the 4-city TSP example, the tour A-B-D-C-A has a total distance of:
In the 4-city TSP example, the tour A-B-C-D-A has a total distance of:
For n cities with a fixed starting city, the number of possible TSP tours is:
questions.explanation: The notes give (n - 1)! tours from a fixed start.
